# Notes on Jeremiah 5

**Gaps.** I only had a few searches and page reads, so some areas are thin:
- I couldn't read Enduring Word past verse 22, or the Pulpit Commentary past verse 24.
- I didn't reach Gill, Ellicott or Precept Austin for most verses.
- I found nothing from the Catholic and Orthodox sites (newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org), netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org or Pentecostal/Lutheran sites, and nothing on prosperity or hyper-grace teaching. Those are left out.
- A few points below come from commentaries I didn't plan to use (Calvin, Clarke, Henry, Barnes). They appeared on Bible Hub and StudyLight pages that collect many commentaries.

## Traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1:**
- The Pulpit Commentary says God would gladly forgive at the slightest sign of real goodness. It says the "man" Jeremiah searches for is someone whose actions and aims are right, like Diogenes looking for an honest man with his lantern. The prophet is speaking for effect, since he and his followers were themselves such men. It renders the key words as "justice" and "good faith," the basic virtues of a society. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/5.htm
- Guzik (Enduring Word) also makes the Diogenes comparison. He says the claim may be exaggeration for effect, but could also be literally true. He applies it to Christ, the one Man who can save a city or a person from judgment. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-5/
- Bible Hub's cross-references link the verse to Ezekiel 9:4. It also links it to Abraham pleading for Sodom in Genesis 18:26. https://biblehub.com/jeremiah/5-1.htm ; https://biblehub.com/catholic/jeremiah/5-1.htm

**v. 2:**
- Pulpit: they use the most solemn oath there is, but they swear falsely. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/5.htm
- Guzik: Jerusalem had plenty of religious people who used the Lord's name, but no one who sought Him sincerely. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-5/

**v. 3:**
- Pulpit: God looks for and demands good faith. This picks up the search in v. 1. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/5.htm
- Guzik quotes Spurgeon: "truth" here means truthfulness in the heart and life, not doctrine. He also quotes Trapp: being unmoved by public judgments is a mark of a false believer. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-5/
- Precept Austin lists two Spurgeon sermons on this verse, "Decided Ungodliness" and "Truthfulness." https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah_commentaries

**v. 4:**
- Pulpit: better translated "they act foolishly." Their lack of religious teaching is why they behave badly. "Judgment" here effectively means religious law. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/5.htm
- Guzik: Jeremiah first assumes the poor are simply uneducated. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-5/
- Precept Austin: the poor still acted wrongly by swearing falsely, refusing to repent and rejecting correction. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-5-commentary

**v. 5:**
- Pulpit: the "bonds" are the straps that tie the yoke to the neck. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/5.htm
- Guzik: the leaders turned out to be rebels too, just educated ones. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-5/

**v. 6:**
- Pulpit:
  - The lion, wolf and leopard are pictures of the cruel invaders.
  - "Wolf of the deserts" is the better reading. Luther translated it the same way.
  - Dante's three beasts were drawn from this verse.
  - Rashi and Jerome read the beasts as the Chaldeans, Persians and Greeks.

  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/5.htm
- Guzik:
  - Most take the animals as the invaders. They could also show cities left empty to wild animals, as threatened in Leviticus 26:22.
  - He quotes Feinberg (strength, ravenous hunger and speed as Babylonian traits) and Trapp (Nebuchadnezzar as lion, wolf and leopard).

  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-5/

**v. 7:**
- Pulpit: "Why should I pardon thee?" Ewald reads "fed them to the full." Pulpit itself prefers the standard Hebrew text, "made them swear," which could point to the oath at Sinai or the one made under Josiah. The adultery may be both literal and spiritual. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/5.htm
- Guzik: ingratitude makes the sin worse. Worship of pagan gods involved ritual prostitution, so spiritual and sexual adultery went together. "By troops" pictures people lining up as if in an army. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-5/

**v. 8:**
- Pulpit: "fed horses" has strong support, though "lustful horses" is possible. The next Hebrew word is very hard, and modern scholars often translate it "roving about." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/5.htm

**v. 9:**
- Guzik: Jeremiah's search found no righteous people, only rebels and adulterers. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-5/
- Precept Austin's outline heads the chapter "Shall Not My Soul Be Avenged?", taken from this verse. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah_commentaries

**v. 10:**
- Pulpit: there is debate over whether to read "walls" or "vine-rows." Judah's corrupt members will be cut away, but the vine-stock will be left. This is Jeremiah's theme of a surviving remnant. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/5.htm
- Guzik: this is a promise of restoration, partly fulfilled under Ezra and Nehemiah. He quotes Harrison linking the cut branches to John 15:1–6. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-5/
- Precept Austin lists a Spurgeon sermon on this verse, "Storming the Battlements." https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah_commentaries

**v. 11:**
- Guzik takes vv. 10–13 together; see v. 10. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-5/

**v. 12:**
- Pulpit: "It is not he" means "it is not He who speaks through the prophets." The people did not deny God exists; they were practical unbelievers. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/5.htm
- Guzik: false prophets "lied about the LORD" when they said trouble wasn't His warning, even if they meant well. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-5/

**v. 13:**
- Pulpit: the unbelieving people are still speaking. They throw back at true prophets the same charge Jeremiah makes against false ones. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/5.htm
- Guzik: the prophets are "wind," movement with no substance. He notes that several commentators think the people are calling the true prophets windbags. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-5/

**v. 14:**
- Guzik: against the prophets of wind, Jeremiah becomes a prophet of fire. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-5/
- Pulpit points the reader to its notes on Jeremiah 1:9–10. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/5.htm

**v. 15:**
- Pulpit:
  - After the northern kingdom fell, Judah stood for all of Israel.
  - "Mighty" is better rendered "ever-replenished."
  - The description would fit the Scythians, but also the Chaldeans.
  - It links the foreign language to Deuteronomy 28:49–50.

  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/5.htm
- Guzik: fulfilled by Babylon under Nebuchadnezzar. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-5/

**v. 16:**
- Pulpit: the quiver is full of deadly arrows; compare Psalm 5:9. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/5.htm
- Guzik quotes Feinberg: every arrow would kill someone. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-5/

**v. 17:**
- Pulpit: "they shall eat thy sons and thy daughters." "Sword" can mean any weapon of war, so the enemy will batter the fortified cities. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/5.htm

**v. 18:**
- Guzik: God repeats His promise not to forsake His covenant people. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-5/

**v. 19:**
- Pulpit: the punishment matches the sin. They served foreign gods in God's land, so they will serve foreigners in a land not their own. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/5.htm
- Guzik reads it the same way. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-5/
- Precept Austin points out the repeated word "serve." https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah_30_commentary

**v. 21:**
- Pulpit: "without understanding" is literally "without heart." Deliberate sin warps a person's moral sense: the prophet states the result here and the cause in v. 23. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/5.htm
- Precept Austin notes that Mark 8:18 alludes to this verse. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/60685

**v. 22:**
- Pulpit: "Me" is placed first for emphasis. "Perpetual decree" shows that Bible writers recognised natural laws, as descriptions of how God works. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/5.htm
- Precept Austin lists a Spurgeon sermon on vv. 22–23, "God's Barrier Against Man's Sin." Its devotional notes say the sea keeps its boundary but God's people did not. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah_commentaries ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah_devotionals-1

**v. 23:**
- Pulpit: the heart is "revolting" when it turns back from God's law, and "rebellious" when it actively defies Him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/5.htm

**v. 24:**
- Ellicott: there aren't two separate rainy seasons; the early rains are autumn and the latter rains close the season in spring. He sees a "natural theology" argument: v. 22 was about law in nature, this verse is about its regular cycle. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/5-24.htm
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: the "weeks of harvest" are the seven weeks between Passover and Pentecost, and God kept rain away during them. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jer/Jer_005.cfm

**v. 25:**
- Pulpit: judgment isn't only future; a foretaste has already come. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/5.htm
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: the nation's guilt had held back the blessings of v. 24. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jer/Jer_005.cfm
- Arthur Pink uses the verse to show that disobedience blocks prayer. https://www.preceptaustin.org/profiting-from-the-word-arthur-pink

**vv. 26–29:** Apart from v. 28, which Precept Austin's devotional reads as short-term pleasure bringing long-term loss (https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah_devotionals-1), I couldn't read any commentary on these verses.

**vv. 30–31:**
- Guzik:
  - The priests ruling "by their own power" is leadership of man, not of God; compare Matthew 20:25–26.
  - Being popular with God's people is never proof that someone speaks for the Lord.

  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-5/
- Barnes: the priests govern according to the false prophecies. False teaching makes God's law feel lighter and takes away the fear of God, and people are content with that. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/5-31.htm
- Pulpit: Jeremiah says the governed were as much to blame as their rulers. https://biblehub.com/jeremiah/5-31.htm
- Gill: the word may mean "princes," who governed under the false prophets' direction. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/5-31.html

## Where the traditions differ (only what I found)

- **v. 24, Baptist (Spurgeon).** Spurgeon's sermon reads the "latter rain" spiritually:
  - Just as the land depends on rain, believers depend on showers of grace.
  - The church needs "the shower of revival."
  - Believers often receive a second, remarkable visitation of the Holy Spirit in later years, which readies them for heaven.

  https://www.ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons15.xxxiii.html

  By contrast, Ellicott and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown stick to farming and climate (links above). I found no Pentecostal source on "latter rain" to compare.
- **v. 31, Reformed (Calvin, Geneva Bible).** Calvin says the priests and false prophets worked hand in glove: without the prophets, the priests would have lost their hold on the people. The Geneva note says disorder is unavoidable when ministers are corrupt. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/5-31.html ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/5-31.htm
- **v. 31, Methodist (Adam Clarke).** Clarke is close to Calvin. The people are happy because they can keep sinning without rebuke, and they would not listen to any reformer. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/5-31.html
- **v. 31, Matthew Henry (an English dissenter).** The people want a loose rein. Leaders who leave them alone in their sins are left alone in theirs. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/5-31.html
- **vv. 1–31, total depravity.** Precept Austin lists a video under this title on the chapter, saying people will increasingly choose sin over righteousness. The page doesn't name the speaker. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah_commentaries

## Other views

- **v. 6, early church and Jewish reading.** Through the Pulpit Commentary: Jerome and Rashi read the three beasts as three empires (Chaldeans, Persians, Greeks). Modern interpreters read them as general calamities. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/5.htm
- **v. 1, Catholic translations.** The Douay-Rheims and Vulgate say "seeketh faith" where most English Bibles say "truth." https://biblehub.com/jeremiah/5-1.htm
